labelScope.description:
Restrict the grant to specific FOLDERS, by name. Send `null` to share the whole mailbox — and note that OMITTING the field is a different request from sending null; see below.

A folder-scoped grant may carry up to `lrswit` — everything `read_write` means. Within the granted folders it reads, marks read/unread privately, changes flags, files messages in, and trashes them. Two letters are rejected, naming themselves: `e` (permanently delete trashed messages), because a purge is irreversible and reaches messages filed in folders the holder cannot see; and `a` (manage folders), because a folder they created would not be inside their own grant.

**What trashing means on a folder-scoped grant.** It removes the message from the folders they were granted — never from the mailbox. A message filed elsewhere as well stays exactly where you put it and simply leaves their view; a message that was only in their folders goes to Trash, where your normal 14-day undo reaches it. They can never permanently delete anything.

**Filing in.** They must name one of their folders; there is no default (yours is INBOX, which is usually not one of theirs). Your filters do not run on what they file — a rule of yours could otherwise move it somewhere they cannot see, forward it, or send an auto-reply in your name.

The grant follows the folder if it is RENAMED, and does not follow the name: deleting a folder and creating a new one with the same name does not revive an old grant. The grant follows the folder into DELETION too: deleting a folder removes it from every grant that names it, and a grant left naming no folders is revoked outright — a share dies with its last folder. An empty list is rejected on WRITE — revoke with DELETE instead.

**Omitting the field and sending `null` are different requests.** On a grant that is already folder-scoped, omitting `labelScope` PRESERVES the existing folders and changes only the rights; sending an explicit `null` is what widens the grant to the whole mailbox. Widening is a deliberate act, so it has to be spelled — otherwise any client that does not know about folder scopes (IMAP `SETACL` among them, since the ACL wire format cannot express one) would silently replace a one-folder grant with a whole-store grant, and drop the `lrs` cap along with it.

On READ an empty list can appear only on the OWNER's listing, and only as residue: it means every folder the grant named has since been deleted and the automatic revocation above could not run. Such a grant is dead — it matches nothing and gives access to nothing — and the owner's listing shows it so you can see it and remove it, while the shared-with-me listing never lists it. It is the one value you cannot send back unchanged: send DELETE, which is what a grant scoped to no folders already means.

A folder-scoped viewer sees only these folders, and only their messages: listings, searches and conversations are all confined to them. Reachable over IMAP, the REST API and JMAP alike.

**Changing a grant signs their clients out of sync.** Sync tokens on a folder-scoped grant are tied to the grant itself, so editing the folders or the rights makes every outstanding token stale exactly once: their clients re-list and carry on. Any live event stream they hold is closed at the same moment, so a narrowed grant takes effect immediately rather than when their connection happens to drop.

Null means the whole mailbox is shared.

mailboxId.description: ULID of the mailbox being shared (the owner's store)

rights.description:
What the person you shared with is allowed to do, written as a set of letters in any order (stored and returned in the canonical order below).

| Letter | Allows |
| --- | --- |
| `l` | See the mailbox in folder listings |
| `r` | Read messages |
| `s` | Change the read/unread mark — each person's own, never shared |
| `w` | Change other flags, such as flagged or answered |
| `i` | Put messages in: append, copy in, move in |
| `t` | Move messages to trash |
| `e` | Permanently delete trashed messages |
| `a` | Create, rename and delete labels |

Instead of letters you may send a preset name, which is usually what you want: `read` or `read_only` (= `lrs`), `read_write` (= `lrswit`), or `admin` / `full` (= `lrswitea`). Hyphenated spellings work too (`read-only`, `read-write`).

**Two things no grant ever allows.** It does not allow sending mail as the mailbox owner. And it does not allow re-sharing: despite the letter, `a` is *not* RFC 4314's ACL-administration right — it means label management here — so only the mailbox owner and account administrators can change who has access.

Letters outside the table (RFC 4314's `p`, `k` and `x`, and the obsolete `c` and `d`) are rejected and named back to you rather than ignored, so a grant never quietly means less than what you asked for. A repeated letter is rejected for the same reason.

A folder-scoped grant may carry up to `lrswit` — everything `read_write` means. Within the granted folders it reads, marks read/unread privately, changes flags, files messages in, and trashes them. Two letters are rejected, naming themselves: `e` (permanently delete trashed messages), because a purge is irreversible and reaches messages filed in folders the holder cannot see; and `a` (manage folders), because a folder they created would not be inside their own grant.

**What trashing means on a folder-scoped grant.** It removes the message from the folders they were granted — never from the mailbox. A message filed elsewhere as well stays exactly where you put it and simply leaves their view; a message that was only in their folders goes to Trash, where your normal 14-day undo reaches it. They can never permanently delete anything.

**Filing in.** They must name one of their folders; there is no default (yours is INBOX, which is usually not one of theirs). Your filters do not run on what they file — a rule of yours could otherwise move it somewhere they cannot see, forward it, or send an auto-reply in your name.

The grant follows the folder if it is RENAMED, and does not follow the name: deleting a folder and creating a new one with the same name does not revive an old grant. The grant follows the folder into DELETION too: deleting a folder removes it from every grant that names it, and a grant left naming no folders is revoked outright — a share dies with its last folder. An empty list is rejected on WRITE — revoke with DELETE instead.

**Omitting the field and sending `null` are different requests.** On a grant that is already folder-scoped, omitting `labelScope` PRESERVES the existing folders and changes only the rights; sending an explicit `null` is what widens the grant to the whole mailbox. Widening is a deliberate act, so it has to be spelled — otherwise any client that does not know about folder scopes (IMAP `SETACL` among them, since the ACL wire format cannot express one) would silently replace a one-folder grant with a whole-store grant, and drop the `lrs` cap along with it.

On READ an empty list can appear only on the OWNER's listing, and only as residue: it means every folder the grant named has since been deleted and the automatic revocation above could not run. Such a grant is dead — it matches nothing and gives access to nothing — and the owner's listing shows it so you can see it and remove it, while the shared-with-me listing never lists it. It is the one value you cannot send back unchanged: send DELETE, which is what a grant scoped to no folders already means.

A folder-scoped viewer sees only these folders, and only their messages: listings, searches and conversations are all confined to them. Reachable over IMAP, the REST API and JMAP alike.

**Changing a grant signs their clients out of sync.** Sync tokens on a folder-scoped grant are tied to the grant itself, so editing the folders or the rights makes every outstanding token stale exactly once: their clients re-list and carry on. Any live event stream they hold is closed at the same moment, so a narrowed grant takes effect immediately rather than when their connection happens to drop.

At most 32 folders may be named in one grant.

rights.description:
What the person you shared with is allowed to do, written as a set of letters in any order (stored and returned in the canonical order below).

| Letter | Allows |
| --- | --- |
| `l` | See the mailbox in folder listings |
| `r` | Read messages |
| `s` | Change the read/unread mark — each person's own, never shared |
| `w` | Change other flags, such as flagged or answered |
| `i` | Put messages in: append, copy in, move in |
| `t` | Move messages to trash |
| `e` | Permanently delete trashed messages |
| `a` | Create, rename and delete labels |

And it does not allow re-sharing: despite the letter, `a` is *not* RFC 4314's ACL-administration right — it means label management here — so only the mailbox owner and account administrators can change who has access.

Letters outside the table (RFC 4314's `p`, `k` and `x`, and the obsolete `c` and `d`) are rejected and named back to you rather than ignored, so a grant never quietly means less than what you asked for. A repeated letter is rejected for the same reason.

bearerAuth.description:
Two credential kinds share this scheme; `GET /api/v1/auth/whoami` answers which one you hold and what it reaches.

**`oek_…` API key** (minted by `POST /api/v1/api-keys`; shown once at mint). `role: account` reaches the full account surface: the directory (domains, routes, patterns, api-keys, accounts, address lists) plus every mailbox the account owns. `role: system` additionally reaches the operator surface, which is documented separately.

**`oemp_…` mailbox app password** (minted by `POST /api/v1/identities/{identityId}/credentials`). Reaches ONE mailbox: its messages, labels, threads, search, sync, send, filters and PIM collections. Directory routes refuse it with `403 insufficient_scope`.

Refusal vocabulary: a missing, malformed, expired, or revoked credential answers `401 unauthorized` with a `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer` challenge; a VALID credential outside its scope answers `403` (`insufficient_scope` for an app password on a directory route, `system_credentials_required` where only the operator may call). The public routes (health, branding, token-in-path capabilities) declare `security: []`.

info.description:
Message store + routing core for the open.email platform: mailbox Durable Objects, R2 blobs, D1 directory.

**Pre-release.** Version 0.x: the surface is complete, but names and shapes may still change without a deprecation cycle. Pin the exact contract you built against.

## Authentication
Bearer credentials, two kinds (the `bearerAuth` security scheme carries the full matrix): an `oek_…` account API key reaches the account's directory and every mailbox it owns; an `oemp_…` mailbox app password reaches ONE mailbox and is refused on directory routes with `403 insufficient_scope`. `GET /api/v1/auth/whoami` answers which credential you hold. A missing or invalid credential answers `401 unauthorized` with a `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer` challenge. The only unauthenticated operations are the ones declared `security: []`: `GET /api/v1/health`; the token-in-path capabilities (`/pim/feeds/{token}`, `/deliveries/fetch/{token}`, `/forwarding/disable/{token}`), where the token IS the credential; and the public `/branding/*` reads a login screen needs before anyone signs in (which answer a uniform 404 for an unknown domain and an unbranded one alike).

## Errors
Every non-2xx answers `{ "error": "snake_case_code", … }`; request-schema failures answer `{ "error": "validation_failed", "issues": [...] }`. Key on the CODE, never on the status alone: the per-operation descriptions say which codes are permanent and which must be retried.

## Rate limits and retries
A `429` is always temporary: retry, never surface it as a permanent failure. Where the wait is known it carries a `Retry-After` header (seconds) and `retryAfterSeconds` in the body. Sending endpoints take an `X-Delivery-Id` idempotency key: retry with the SAME id and the platform converges on one send.

## Pagination, ids, timestamps
Listings page with opaque cursors (`nextCursor`, absent on the last page); hold filters and sort constant across a crawl. Ids are ULIDs. Timestamps are epoch SECONDS everywhere, with one deliberate exception: the RFC 8621 search filter's `before`/`after` take UTCDate strings.

## Getting started
1. Create an API key (from the console, or `POST /api/v1/api-keys` with an existing key), then `GET /api/v1/auth/whoami`.
2. `GET /api/v1/identities` lists your mailboxes; message routes take the mailbox's ULID.
3. Read: `GET /mailboxes/{mailboxId}/messages`, then `/messages/{id}/content`.
4. Send: `POST /mailboxes/{mailboxId}/send`.
5. Stay current: poll `GET /mailboxes/{mailboxId}/messages/changes`, or subscribe to the WebSocket at `/mailboxes/{mailboxId}/events`.

## Webhooks
The HTTP callbacks this platform POSTS OUT (event notifications, message deliveries to webhook addresses) are specified in this document's top-level `webhooks` section, signature scheme included.

## Push
Three channels wake a client, by where it runs. A foreground client holds the WebSocket (`GET /mailboxes/{mailboxId}/events`). A server subscribes an event webhook (above). A device that must wake while the app is closed registers Web Push (RFC 8030): browsers, PWAs and UnifiedPush Android apps subscribe with the `vapidPublicKey` from `GET /push-subscriptions` as `applicationServerKey`, register the resulting endpoint at `POST /push-subscriptions`, and echo back the verification code the first push delivers. Every push is content-free: a `StateChange` whose per-type state tokens are accepted verbatim as `since` by `GET /mailboxes/{mailboxId}/messages/changes`. A native app with its own backend combines the first two instead: receive event webhooks server-side, wake the app through your own APNs/FCM credentials, then sync via the changes feed. The platform deliberately holds no third-party push credentials, so there is no APNs or FCM bridge to configure here.

get.description:
Upgrades to a WebSocket that streams best-effort change signals for this mailbox: message.new (delivery), message.updated / message.expunged / message.restored / message.purged, label.expunged (IMAP EXPUNGE), label.created / label.renamed / label.deleted, trash.emptied, thread.merged (an arrival joined two conversations — re-list thread views, since thread ids are convergent rather than stable), and state.changed. Each frame is `{ v, type, ts, data }` with identifiers only — never message content. The vocabulary is additive: treat an unrecognized `type` as a generic 'something changed' nudge rather than an error.

Signals are not a journal: there is no replay or backlog, so on every (re)connect re-sync and treat each event as 'this changed, re-fetch it'. A `state.changed` frame carries the current state token for each type (`{ Email, Mailbox, Thread, EmailDelivery }`); its `Email` value is exactly what `GET /mailboxes/{mailboxId}/messages/changes` accepts as `since`, so a client can re-sync incrementally instead of re-listing. A `ready` frame with the session deadline is sent on connect; the session is closed with code 4401 (session_expired — reconnect with a fresh bearer) after 12h, 4403 (credential_revoked — the app password was revoked; do not reconnect with it) or 4410 (mailbox_gone — stop reconnecting). Keepalive: send a `ping` text frame, receive `pong`.

get.description:
Answers `created` / `updated` / `destroyed` message ids for everything that happened since `since`, plus a `newState` to send next time. Ids only: fetch what you need through the ordinary message endpoints.

**The loop.** Call once with no `since` to get a starting `newState`; do your full listing; then poll with `since=<newState>`, or better, subscribe to `GET /mailboxes/{mailboxId}/events` and call this whenever a frame arrives (a `state.changed` frame's `Email` value is itself a valid `since`). Keep calling while `hasMore` is true.

**What maps to what.** A delivery is `created`, and so is a restore from trash. Flag, keyword and label changes are `updated`, as is a message whose conversation was merged into another. An expunge (soft delete to trash) and a purge are both `destroyed` — this feed mirrors the ordinary live listing, so use `?state=expunged` if you present a trash view. The feed errs toward telling you too much: a message may be reported `created` where `updated` would have done, which costs one refetch. It never reports a message you still hold as `destroyed`.

**When the token is too old** (or was minted by a mailbox that has since been rebuilt) you get `410 cannot_calculate_changes`. There is no repair: re-list the mailbox and bootstrap a fresh token. History is kept for 30 days, comfortably longer than the 14-day trash window, so this only happens to a client that has been away a long time.

Sending one grant replaces any previous grant for that identity, so this is how you widen or narrow access as well as how you create it. Both parties must belong to the same account, and a mailbox cannot be shared with itself.

post.description: POSTed to the URL configured by `PUT /api/v1/mailboxes/{mailboxId}/event-webhook` or `PUT /api/v1/domains/{domain}/event-webhook` (all events, no filters; the mailbox and domain hooks each get their own copy, signed with their own secret). Answer a 2xx within 30 seconds; acknowledge first, work after. Redirects are never followed: a 3xx counts as a failed attempt at the registered URL. A non-2xx answer or a timeout is a failed attempt, retried on a backoff ladder with the SAME batch `id` (dedupe on it); 24 hours of consecutive failures auto-disables the hook (`disabledReason: "failing"` on the resource) and any PUT re-enables it. Events are best-effort signals, not a journal: after re-enabling (or any suspected gap), re-sync through `GET /mailboxes/{mailboxId}/messages/changes` using the `states.Email` token. Requests carry `User-Agent: openemail-events/1`.

post.description: POSTed when mail arrives for an address routed to a webhook URL (`POST /api/v1/routes` with a webhook target), or as a TAP beside an ordinary mailbox delivery. The POST *is* the delivery: answer a 2xx within 30 seconds (acknowledge first, work after) or the attempt is retried with the same `deliveryId`. Redirects are never followed: a 3xx counts as a failed attempt at the registered URL. Bodies and attachments are inlined up to fixed ceilings (1 MiB per body, 256 KiB per attachment, 1 MiB total attachment budget); anything larger arrives as a signed, expiring `url` / `rawUrl` capability redeemed at `GET /api/v1/deliveries/fetch/{token}` with no credential. The parse is the SAME machinery as `GET /messages/{id}/content`, so a webhook receiver and a REST reader can never disagree about what the body is.
